On 1 November 2011, [Mario Draghi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Draghi "Mario Draghi") replaced Jean-Claude Trichet as President of the ECB.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-38) This change in leadership also marks the start of a new era under which the ECB will become more and more interventionist and eventually ended the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis").

Draghi's presidency started with the impressive launch of a new round of 1% interest loans with a term of three years (36 months) – the **Long-term Refinancing operations (LTRO)**. Under this programme, 523 Banks tapped as much as €489.2 bn (US$640 bn). Observers were surprised by the volume of loans made when it was implemented.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-ECB82011-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-NYTloans-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-NYTNorris-41) By far biggest amount of €325bn was tapped by banks in Greece, Ireland, Italy and Spain.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-42) Although those LTROs loans did not directly benefit EU governments, it effectively allowed banks to do a [carry trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carry_trade "Carry trade"), by lending off the LTROs loans to governments with an interest margin. The operation also facilitated the rollover of €200bn of maturing bank debts[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-43) in the first three months of 2012.

##### "Whatever it takes" (26 July 2012)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: \"Whatever it takes\" (26 July 2012)")]

Facing renewed fears about sovereigns in the eurozone continued Mario Draghi made a decisive speech in London, by declaring that the ECB "...is ready to do _**whatever it takes**_ to preserve the Euro. And believe me, it will be enough."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-44) In light of slow political progress on solving the eurozone crisis, Draghi's statement has been seen as a key turning point in the eurozone crisis, as it was immediately welcomed by European leaders, and led to a steady decline in bond yields for eurozone countries, in particular Spain, Italy and France.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-46)

Following up on Draghi's speech, on 6 September 2012 the ECB announced the **[Outright Monetary Transactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outright_Monetary_Transactions "Outright Monetary Transactions")** programme (OMT).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-47) Unlike the previous SMP programme, OMT has no [ex-ante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex-ante "Ex-ante") time or size limit.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-48) However, the activation of the purchases remains conditioned to the adherence by the benefitting country to an adjustment programme to the ESM. The program was adopted with near unanimity, the Bundesbank president [Jens Weidmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jens_Weidmann "Jens Weidmann") being the sole member of the ECB's Governing Council to vote against it.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-49)

Even if OMT was never actually implemented until today, it made the "Whatever it takes" pledge credible and significantly contributed to stabilizing financial markets and ending the sovereign debt crisis. According to various sources, the OMT programme and "whatever it takes" speeches were made possible because EU leaders previously agreed to build the [banking union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Banking_union "European Banking union").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-50)

### Low inflation and quantitative easing (2015–2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Low inflation and quantitative easing (2015–2019)")]

In November 2014, the bank moved into its [new premises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seat_of_the_European_Central_Bank "Seat of the European Central Bank"), while the [Eurotower building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurotower_(Frankfurt_am_Main) "Eurotower (Frankfurt am Main)") was dedicated to hosting the newly established supervisory activities of the ECB under [European Banking Supervision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Banking_Supervision "European Banking Supervision").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-51)

Although the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis") was almost solved by 2014, the ECB started to face a repeated decline[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-52) in the Eurozone inflation rate, indicating that the economy was going towards a deflation. Responding to this threat, the ECB announced on 4 September 2014 the launch of two bond buying purchases programmes: the Covered Bond Purchasing Programme (CBPP3) and Asset-Backed Securities Programme (ABSPP).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-53)

#### Asset Purchase programme (APP)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Asset Purchase programme (APP)")]

On 22 January 2015, the ECB announced an extension of those programmes within a full-fledge "[quantitative easing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_easing "Quantitative easing")" programme which also included sovereign bonds, to the tune of 60 billion euros per month up until at least September 2016. The programme was started on 9 March 2015.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-54)

On 8 June 2016, the ECB added corporate bonds to its asset purchases portfolio with the launch of the corporate sector purchase programme (CSPP).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-55) Under this programme, it conducted the net purchase of corporate bonds until January 2019 to reach about €177 billion. While the programme was halted for 11 months in January 2019, the ECB restarted net purchases in November 2019.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-56)

On 5 May 2020, the Court ordered the [Bundestag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundestag "Bundestag") and the [Bundesregierung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Germany "Cabinet of Germany") to ensure the ECB had carried out a proportionality assessment of the vast purchases of government debt in the [Public Sector Purchase Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Sector_Purchase_Programme?action=edit&redlink=1 "Public Sector Purchase Programme (page does not exist)") (PSPP) to ensure the economic and fiscal policy effects do not outweigh its policy objectives.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Camous-2020b-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bundesverfassungsgericht-2023-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2020c-60) The PSPP-implementing decision has been considered an act [ultra vires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_vires "Ultra vires") by the ECB as it was too arbitrary and lacks reasoning in ints proportionality assessment.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bundesverfassungsgericht-2023-58)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-62) This ruling by the German Constitutional Court comes at a difficult time for the ECB as it was at the time considering expanding the PEPP. The ruling also reflects the mistrust within some parts of Germany in the ECB, which is seen there as an institution that bails out profligate Southern European countries.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2020c-60) Moreover, this ruling also highlights the vital problem on the euro area architecture, as the range of instruments can use to fulfil its mandate remains unclear.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Camous-2020b-57)

As of 2021,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit) the size of the ECB's quantitative easing programme had reached 2947 billion euros.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-63)

#### Long Term Refinancing Operations (LTRO)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Long Term Refinancing Operations (LTRO)")]

The long term refinancing operations (LTRO) are regular open market operations providing financing to credit institutions for periods up to four years. They aim at favoring lending conditions to the private sector and more generally stimulating bank lending to the real economy,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-64) thereby fostering growth.

In December 2011 and January 2012, in the aftermath of the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), the ECB implemented two LTROs, injecting over €1000 billion of liquidity in the Eurozone financial system. They were later criticized for their inability to revive growth and to help truly revive the real economy, despite having stabilized the Eurozone's financial institutions.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Fontan-2018-65) Further, these operations were devoid of monitoring from the ECB regarding the use made of these liquidities[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Fontan-2018-65) and it appeared that banks had significantly used these funds to pursue carry-trade strategies,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-66) purchasing sovereign bonds with higher rates and corresponding maturity to generate profits, instead of increasing private lending.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Fontan-2018-65)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Dwyer-2023-67)

These critics and deficiencies brought the ECB to instigate targeted long term refinancing operations (TLTROs), first in September and later in December 2014.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-68) These complementary programs imposed conditionality on the LTROs.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Fontan-2018-65) The TLTROs provided low cost financing to participating banks, under the condition that they reached certain targets in terms of lending to firms and households.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Dwyer-2023-67) The participating banks were thus more incited to lend to the real economy.

A third wave of TLTRO's was announced on 7 March 2019, namely the TLTRO III.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-69) Under TLTRO III, the interest rate was set at −0.5% below the deposit facility rate (DFR), under condition that banks reached a specific lending performance threshold. The TLTRO III programme was successful to stimulate credit growth.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Barmeier-2023-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-71)

### Christine Lagarde's era (2019 – )

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Christine Lagarde's era (2019 – )")]

In July 2019, EU leaders nominated [Christine Lagarde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Lagarde "Christine Lagarde") to replace Mario Draghi as ECB President. Lagarde resigned from her position as managing director of the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") in July 2019[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-72) and formally took over the ECB's presidency on 1 November 2019.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-73)

Lagarde immediately signalled a change of style in the ECB's leadership. She embarked the ECB on a strategic review of the ECB's monetary policy strategy, an exercise the ECB had not done for 17 years. As part of this exercise, Lagarde committed the ECB to look into how monetary policy could contribute to [address climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation"),[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-74) and promised that "no stone would be left unturned." The ECB president also adopted a change of communication style, in particular in her use of social media to promote gender equality,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-75) and by opening dialogue with civil society stakeholders.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-77)

#### The ECB's response to COVID-19 pandemic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: The ECB's response to COVID-19 pandemic")]

The onset of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") precipitated an unprecedented crisis, profoundly impacting global public health, economies, and societal structures on an unparalleled scale. The crisis led to renewed tensions in European sovereign bonds markets, marked by a growing spreads between the interest rates paid by Eurozone member states,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Runkel-2022-78) which spurred concerns about the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis").

On 12 March 2020, the ECB announced a set of policy measures such as an additional package of net asset purchases of €120 billion by the end of 2020 under the already existing APP, and more favorable terms on the TLTRO III. During the press conference, Christine Lagarde declared that the ECB "[...] is not here to close spreads."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Tesche-2022b-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Lagarde-2020c-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Balmer-2020b-81) This particular statement triggered a sudden negative reaction on financial markets, with a widening of yield spreads in Spain, Italy and Greece.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Moessner-2022-82)

##### Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP)")]

On 19 March 2020—less than one week after Lagarde's unfortunate statements on the spreads—the ECB announced by surprise the launch of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) worth €750 billion to boost liquidity in the European economy and to contain any sharp increases in sovereign yield spreads.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sciorilli_Borrelli-2020c-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-84) This announcement led to an immediate reboot in stock prices[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Moessner-2022-82)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ortmans-2021-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Benigno-2022-86) and came one day after the spike of sovereign risk spreads.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Alberola-2022-87)

The PEPP was designed as a typical "[quantitative easing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_easing "Quantitative easing")" policy, under which the ECB is able to purchase securities from the private and public sector in a flexible manner.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2020d-88)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Tesche-2022b-79)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bertoldi-2023c-89) The purpose of the PEPP was to stabilize sovereign bonds yields to low and stable levels, thus preventing self-fulfilling panics in financial markets as was the case during the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Tesche-2020a-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Carnazza-2021-91)

The PEPP was established as a separate purchase programme alongside the pre-existing Asset Purchase Programme (APP) with the sole purpose to respond to the economic and financial consequences of the COVID-19 crisis, and in particular prevent market fragmentations.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-DB-2023-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Grund-2020-93) While very similar, contrary to the APP, the ECB decided to allow itself to deviate from the capital key. This temporal flexibility from the capital key meant that the ECB could more effectively prevent the rise of Italian and Spanish yield spreads.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Tesche-2020a-90)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Borri-2021-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Blotevogel-2023-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-96)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Camous-2020b-57)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-97)

Assets meeting the eligibility criteria of the APP were also eligible under the PEPP.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2023-98) However, the pool of assets eligible under the PEPP was broader than the usual ECB collateral eligibility framework.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sciorilli_Borrelli-2020c-83) For instance, Greek sovereign bonds could be purchased by the ECB under this programme, despite having a credit ratings below the usual investment grade requirement.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sciorilli_Borrelli-2020c-83)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-FT-2023b-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2020e-100) This waiver was given based on several considerations from the ECB: there was a need to alleviate the pressures stemming from the pandemic on the Greek financial markets; Greece was already and would be closely monitored by giving the waiver; and Greece regained market access.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Boninghausen-2022b-101) Non-financial commercial paper with a remaining maturity of at least 28 days were also eligible for purchase under the PEPP.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2023-98)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-102)

On 4 June 2020, the ECB announced[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-103) it would expand the PEPP by another €600 billion,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Pinto-2023-104) as it became clear that the pandemic would continue to harm European economies.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Runkel-2022-78)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2020d-88)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Benigno-2022-86)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Moessner-2022-82) Half a year later, on 10 December 2020, the ECB announced its final expansion of the PEPP worth another €500 billion, totalling the final PEPP to €1.850 trillion,[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2020a-105)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-DB-2023-92)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Alberola-2022-87) corresponding to 15.4% of the euro-area GDP of 2019.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wieland-2023-106)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/PEPP_Graph_Improved.png/250px-PEPP_Graph_Improved.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PEPP_Graph_Improved.png)

Gross securities purchases by the ECB under the PEPP[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-ECB-2023-107)

In December 2021, the ECB announced that it would discontinue net purchases under the PEPP as from the end of March 2022 and that it intended to reinvest the principal payments from maturing securities at least until the end of 2024.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-109)

On 31 March 2022, at the end of the net purchases, the net purchases amounted to €1.718 billion, of which €1.665 billion is invested in public sector securities and €52 billion in private sector securities.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Boninghausen-2022a-110) Of the total €1.850 billion available under the PEPP, 93% of the full envelope wase used, due to indications of decreased financial stress in the Euro Area, mainly thanks to relaxation of COVID restrictions and the reopening of European markets.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-111)

#### Criticism against PEPP

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Criticism against PEPP")]

Overall, the PEPP programme was widely welcomed by market participants and European policy makers. However in March 2021, a group of German economists and lawyers filed a lawsuit against the PEPP at the [German Federal Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Constitutional_Court "Federal Constitutional Court").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Tesche-2022b-79)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108)

##### New TLTRO III and PELTROs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: New TLTRO III and PELTROs")]

On 30 April 2020, the ECB Governing council introduced additional measures to support the economy during the COVID-19 pandemic, including PELTROs and new modalities for the TLTROs.

First, the ECB made several adjustments to the framework of its TLTRO III.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2020c-112) A key change was that the ECB also reduced the interest rate applied to these open market operations to a rate going as low as −1% for the banks meeting the lending threshold of 0%.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2020c-112) With the TLTRO III, the participating banks were thus enabled to borrow at lower interest rates than those paid on their excess reserve.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Castillo_Lozoya-2022-113) Another key change was thet ECB's decision to expand bank's borrowing allowance under TLTRO III from 30% to 50%, then up to 55% of their portfolio of loans to firms and households.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-114)

Second, the ECB introduced pandemic emergency long-term refinancing operations (PELTROs).[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-ECB_press_release,_30_April_2020-115) The market operations are similar to the TLTRO III, but are conduced in a more frequent basis in order to ensure smooth liquidity provision to the market.

During the pandemic, these monetary responses proved essential. In their absence, a credit crunch would normally have taken place. Indeed, increase in demand traditionally translates in a rise of borrowing costs.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Altavilla-2023-116) Reports from various member states central banks on the matter indicate that loans supply by participating banks has indeed expanded, in line with the ECB policy.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Barmeier-2023-70)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Castillo_Lozoya-2022-113)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-117) Accordingly, thorough academic studies have confirmed the actual enhancement of financing conditions and the avoidance of credit scarcity.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Altavilla-2023-116)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-118) In fact, the credit to firms attained unprecedented levels when from March to May 2020, it increased by €250 billion on aggregate.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Altavilla-2023-116) Furthermore, analysts observed that even non-participating banks (to the TLTROs and PELTROs) benefited from it in parallel manners.

#### Transmission Protection instrument (TPI)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Transmission Protection instrument (TPI)")]

The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) is a tool the ECB could use to ensure monetary policy decisions are smoothly transmitted across all euro area countries, introduced on 21 July 2022.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bertoldi-2023c-89)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Broeders-2023c-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2023c-120)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Lengwiler-2023-122) Under the TPI, the ECB would be able to purchase securities in the secondary market, to counter against "unwanted, disorderly market dynamics", self fulfilling crises market expectations that do not reflect reality,[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sandbu-2022-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Callegari-2023-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Spendzharova-2023-125) thus not justified by "country specific fundamentals."[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2023c-120)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Peychev-2022-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2022-127)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-FT-2022-128) The TPI thus enables the ECB to control the difference between borrowing costs across the euro area, thereby reducing fragmentation risk across the euro area.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Broeders-2023c-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2023c-120)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sandbu-2022-123)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-FT-2022-128)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Grimm-2023-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Koranyi-2022-130) By not letting interfere market dynamics that do not reflect economic reality, the ECB fulfils its secondary mandate under the TFEU, namely "to support the general economic policies of the Union."[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2023c-120)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sandbu-2022-123) Although PEPP would remain the first line of defence to counter for transmission risks,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Peychev-2022-126) the TPI should be seen as an addition to the ECB's toolkit.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)

##### Eligible securities under the TPI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Eligible securities under the TPI")]

Contrary to the PEPP and the APP, the TPI does not have an _ex ante_ upper limit on the purchase of securities.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Spendzharova-2023-125)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2022-127)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Grimm-2023-129)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-131) Although the ECB has stated it would primarily buy only government bonds on the secondary market[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Spendzharova-2023-125) maturing between 1 and 10 years,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2022-127) the bonds purchased fall under the complete discretion of the ECB and does not necessarily follow the capital key, and private securities could be considered as well.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-FT-2022-128)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-132) However, there are four conditions that need to be met before securities are eligible for purchasing under TPI:[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Grimm-2023-129)

1.   Compliance with the fiscal framework of the EU and not be involved in the [excessive deficit procedure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_and_Growth_Pact "Stability and Growth Pact");
2.   Absence of macroeconomic imbalances and not being involved in an excessive [macroeconomic imbalance procedure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroeconomic_Imbalance_Procedure "Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure"), demonstrating that it is in compliance with the commission's recommendations;
3.   Sovereign debt trajectory must be sustainable, assessed by the ECB and other relevant bodies;
4.   Stick to commitments made under the Recovery and Resilience Facility, proving that the government follows sound and sustainable macroeconomic policies.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Peychev-2022-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2022-127)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Koranyi-2022-130)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-POLITICO-2022b-133)

The conditions for government bonds to be eligible under the TPI draw heavily on the macroeconomic governance, and making sure that politicians do not take decisions that facilitate speculation.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Sandbu-2022-123)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Martin-2022b-134) The decision by the ECB to support a country by using the TPI will depend on the severity of the risks a country faces.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2022-127)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-POLITICO-2022b-133) Government debt should thus be sustainable to be eligible for TPI purchases.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Callegari-2023-124)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-FT-2022-128)

If the aforementioned conditions are met, the ECB could decide to activate the TPI.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Spendzharova-2023-125)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2022-127)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-135) Purchases will be ended under the TPI either due to increased transmission of monetary policy or the risks have proven to be country-specific.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bank-2022-121) So far, the TPI has not been deployed yet.

##### Effects of and critiques on the TPI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Effects of and critiques on the TPI")]

The TPI enables the Governing Council to a more rapid increase in interest rate,[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Broeders-2023c-119)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108) the first raise in interest rates by the ECB in 11 years.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Bertoldi-2023c-89)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Martin-2022b-134) and the unpredictable nature of market sentiment could justify the reason for ECB-intervention to stabilise the monetary union,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Arnold-2023c-120) more or less the same reasoning as for the PEPP.

However, the relationship between the PEPP and the TPI raises questions as the PEPP would remain the first line of defence against transmission risks.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108) The creation of the TPI seems legally vulnerably: problems in the Euro Area are common and recurring, but it is not automatically the argument to invent a whole new anti-fragmentation tool.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108) With the TPI, the ECB can put pressure on countries by assessing publicly if they are eligible for the TPI, that is assessing whether the government has conducted adequate fiscal policies and structural reforms to deserve the support of the ECB. This endangers the politic neutrality of the ECB.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-136) If ever deployed, the usage of the TPI will spark controversy as the conditions to be deployed are not watertight.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Wellink-2023d-108)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-POLITICO-2022b-133)

##### Strategy Review (2020-2021)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Strategy Review (2020-2021)")]

As a consequence of the COVID-19 crisis, the ECB extended the duration of the strategy review until September 2021. On 13 July 2021, the ECB presented the outcomes of the strategy review, with the main following announcements:

*   The ECB announced a new inflation target of 2% instead of its "close but below two per cent" inflation target. The ECB also made it clear it could overshoot its target under certain circumstances.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Amaro-2021-137)
*   The ECB announced it would try to incorporate the cost of housing (imputed rents) into its inflation measurement
*   The ECB announced an action plan on climate change[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-138)

The ECB also said it would carry out another strategy review in 2025.

### Inflation surge of 2021

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Inflation surge of 2021")]

In the summer of 2021, coinciding with the European Central Bank's announcement of its revised monetary policy framework and its initiative for climate action, the eurozone witnessed a notable [inflationary surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation "2021–2023 inflation"). This resurgence of inflation continued to escalate over the following year, culminating in inflation rates reaching double digits for the first time since the 1970s, a year after the ECB's strategic updates.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139) The inflation rate reached an unprecedented peak of 4.9% in November 2021, marking the highest level since the introduction of the euro.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Baltensperger-2023-140)

#### Framing of the crisis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Framing of the crisis")]

The new era of inflation prompted a significant shift in the European Central Bank's framing compared to its stance in the 2000s. Initially, from its inception until the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), the ECB's primary objective was price stability, adhering to strict institutional rules that minimized policy trade-offs with other goals beyond price stability.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-141)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-142) This approach was rooted in the "Central Bank Independence template", advocating that central bank's limited role to price stability and its independence were optimal.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-143)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Hartmann-2018-144)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-145)

However, the post-financial crisis landscape, especially during the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis") and subsequent economic stagnation era, necessitated a substantial revision in the ECB's strategy.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Hartmann-2018-144) The ECB moved away from its original Central Bank Independence template, leading to a blurring of its objective hierarchy. It adopted new strategies such as acting as a [lender of last resort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lender_of_last_resort "Lender of last resort") for the banking system and fostering growth through very low interest rates and extensive asset purchase programs, which were designed to help stabilize specific market segments and in the end revive growth.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-146)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-147)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-148)

In 2021, the European Central Bank embraced a significant strategic pivot by adopting its Climate Action Plan along with a new monetary policy strategy.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-149) This shift aimed to institutionalize the ECB's evolving role, moving beyond the singular focus on price stability—a policy shaped largely by the aftermath of the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis"). Instead, the ECB began acknowledging its multifaceted responsibilities, which now include maintaining financial stability, supporting economic growth, and addressing climate-related objectives.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139) However, with the [surging of inflation in 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation "2021–2023 inflation"), some wondered as to whether the European Central Bank would revert to its foundational role, predominantly focused on chasing the "inflation monsters". The term "inflation monsters'' echoes the 2010 video of the ECB where two young people are facing a blue inflation monster unleashing banknotes and threatening to wreck the economy.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139) Nevertheless, ECB policymakers effectively drew connections between the Central Bank Independence (CBI) framework and the experiences of the stagflation era to rationalize their decision to increase interest rates, avoiding the need for a discourse on regime change. In doing so, they recognized the complex trade-offs inherent in balancing various macroeconomic objectives and the challenging decisions they had to face.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139)

It was with this new monetary strategy that the eurozone found itself facing rising [inflation in 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation "2021–2023 inflation").[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139) Recent studies stated that key debate among policymakers centered on whether this inflationary trend would be transitory or permanent. Paul Krugman argued that the current inflationary surge would prove to be transitory, whereas other economists such as Olivier Blanchard and Larry Summers had issued warnings regarding the possible persistence of this inflation.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-150) Initially, both the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve misjudged the situation, assuming the inflation spike to be temporary and expecting a swift return to their inflation target. This misperception led to the ECB's initial inaction regarding its [monetary policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy "Monetary policy").[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Storm-151)

#### Response to the 2021 inflation crisis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Response to the 2021 inflation crisis")]

After big increases in the inflation rates throughout 2021 and 2022, the European Central Bank and the FED finally decided to raise their interest rates and abandon their very low interest rates, for the first time since the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis") and the end of the CBI era, as it had become clear the inflationary trend wasn't temporary.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139) This decision came in late July 2022 for the ECB, when the inflation rate in the eurozone was already at 8.9% and had been higher than the 2% target for more than a year, and in March 2022 for the FED.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-152) The European Central Bank's response to the Federal Reserve's actions can partly be attributed to concerns about imported inflation from the USA. Specifically, if the FED increases its policy rates while the ECB remains static, it could lead to a depreciation of the euro against the dollar. Such a scenario would likely result in higher import costs for the eurozone, as many global trade goods are priced in dollars. On the other hand, this would benefit the US economy by making imports from the eurozone cheaper.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-153)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-154)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Moessner-2023-155)

Furthermore, the impact of US dollar appreciation, following the FED's policy rate hikes, tends to be more pronounced in the international inflation rates of energy and food. These commodities are commonly priced in US dollars, making their inflation rates more sensitive to exchange rate variations.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-156) In the European Union, public inflation expectations are significantly influenced by the prices of energy and food. Thus, this form of imported inflation can further exacerbate overall inflation levels of the eurozone.

The ECB also declared its intention to systematically diminish net asset purchases within their asset purchase program (APP) and end them under the pandemic emergency purchase program (PEPP) launched during the COVID crisis by the first trimester of 2022.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Goutsmedt-2023-139) On the other hand, the Federal Reserve initiated the reduction of its asset purchase program in November 2021, to finally stop it by March 2022. The Asset Purchase Programs of the ECB initially boosted asset values on bank balance sheets and led to expectations of lower future short short-term interest rates. These programs also raised inflation expectations, eventually reanchoring long-term inflation expectations. Phasing out the Asset Purchase Programs thus signals alignment with the different policy rate hikes in an attempt to cool down the economy and demonstrates a commitment to combating inflation.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-157)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-158)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-159)

Research indicates that the European Central Bank responded to the escalating inflation more slowly and cautiously than the FED, showing hopes that a moderate tightening of monetary policy would suffice. The ECB was notably slower in acknowledging the mistaken nature of its initial assumption that the inflationary trend would be transitory.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Baltensperger-2023-140) The transition away from extremely low interest rates was soon accompanied by various rate increases, culminating in the ECB's main rate reaching 4% by the end of September.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-160) In contrast, the FED's latest rate hike elevated the Effective Federal Funds Rate to 5.33% in August, underscoring a more aggressive and rapid tightening of monetary policy compared to the ECB's approach.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-161) However, the global monetary tightening cycle turned out to be the most synchronized one in the past half-century. By February 2023, more than 90% of economies had hiked their policy rates. The latest peak of highly synchronized action by central banks was during the 1970s and the oil prices shocks where 70% of them had raised their interest rates.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Moessner-2023-155)

#### Critics regarding the new monetary policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Critics regarding the new monetary policy")]

Criticism first emerged regarding the methodologies used for inflation estimation and their failure to anticipate the inflation surge. A primary critique focused on the inadequacy of traditional tools like the Phillips Curve, which examines the relationship between inflation and certain economic activity indicators, for accurately forecasting inflation.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Storm-151)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Baba-2024-162) During the 1970s, the Phillips Curve also faced significant criticism for its inability to accurately predict the inflation experienced in that decade. This period marked a critical reassessment of the curve's predictive capacity, particularly in the context of the economic phenomena of the time.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-163) Traditional indicators used for forecasting economic dynamics, such as the output and unemployment gaps, were found to be inadequate in signaling the overheating of the economy and the prevailing tight labor market conditions.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Storm-151)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Baba-2024-162)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-164) Moreover, the important belief among central banks that sustained inflationary increases are a consequence of unanchored long-term inflation expectations was challenged during 2021–2022. During this period, inflation expectations remained relatively stable, leading to the misinterpretations by the European Central Bank and other monetary authorities regarding the inflationary trend's nature.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Storm-151) Both the FED and the ECB argued that the rise in inflation was only temporary and was the sole result of post-pandemic supply disruptions on a few selected goods and services (food and energy). The FED and the ECB then maintained their expansionary monetary policy, keeping interest rates low.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Baltensperger-2023-140)

Some critics have also emerged saying that it was complicated for independent central banks, including the ECB, to accurately assess during a synchronized policy rate hike the potential spillovers of cross-countries monetary policy on the inflation. This might lead to excessive monetary tightening (higher interest rates) in unusual circumstances.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Moessner-2023-155)

Concerns have also been raised about the European Central Bank's effectiveness in addressing the recent surge in energy prices.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ider-2023-165) Some experts suggest that the eurozone should be viewed as a small open economy, implying that changes in its demand may not significantly impact global prices. Moreover, they argue that monetary policy might have minimal influence on the global demand for energy. This is because household demand for essentials like heating and transportation is believed to be relatively insensitive to price changes.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ider-2023-165) Additionally, while a stronger euro could theoretically lead to lower import prices, it's uncertain whether these savings would be effectively passed on to consumers.

However, recent studies contradict these views by highlighting the significant role of energy prices in the transmission of monetary policy within the eurozone. An increase in the ECB's policy rates tends to appreciate the euro against the dollar. This appreciation can lead to higher local energy costs but may also reduce demand, potentially lowering global energy prices. These studies support the ECB's decision to follow the Federal Reserve's lead in raising policy rates, which appears to have been a strategic move to curb imported inflation and address the spike in energy prices.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ider-2023-165)

#### Effects of the monetary tightening

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=European_Central_Bank&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Effects of the monetary tightening")]

The implementing a of tighter monetary policy has emerged as the eurozone solution to fight the latest inflationary pressure. However, this approach bears the risk of hindering the progress of the economic revival post-[COVID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ider-2022-166)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Evolution_of_the_MRO_rate_and_the_HICP_for_the_EU.png/250px-Evolution_of_the_MRO_rate_and_the_HICP_for_the_EU.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Evolution_of_the_MRO_rate_and_the_HICP_for_the_EU.png)

Evolution of the MRO rate and the HICP for the EU[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-167)

Raising interest rates is a strategic move by the ECB with specific aims: to decelerate economic activity, stabilize inflation expectations, and steer towards lower inflation levels. Studies have shown that as interest rates rise, the price on the world market does not really change. However, the Euro becomes more attractive to investors, leading to its appreciation against other currencies. This change benefits households paying for gas in Euros, as it translates into lower prices for dollar-traded oil.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ider-2022-166)

On the other hand, the increase in interest rates, while helping to suppress prices, also places strains on the manufacturing sector and the labor market. The aftermath of this shock sees tighter financing conditions and a dip in demand, resulting in a slight uptick in unemployment rates, going beyond 0.1 percentage points. Although the study shows that manufacturing sector quickly rebounds, returning to its pre-shock state within about three months, the impact on unemployment rates lingers for a longer period.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank#cite_note-Ider-2022-166)

# The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area

*   [![Image 2: X](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/twitter-x.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "X")
*   [![Image 3: Facebook](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/facebook.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "Facebook")
*   [![Image 4: Linkedin](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/linkedin.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "Linkedin")
*   [![Image 5: Email](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/mail.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "Email")

16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)

_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_

As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.

Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.

This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.

# The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area

*   [![Image 2: X](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/twitter-x.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "X")

*   [![Image 4: Linkedin](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/linkedin.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "Linkedin")
*   [![Image 5: Email](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/themes/custom/edp/assets/svg/mail.svg)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area# "Email")

16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)

_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_

As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.

Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.

This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.

From 2008 to 2024, the number of bank branches operating across the European Union declined steadily. By 2024, the total had fallen to 106,571 - representing a reduction of over 100,000 branches since the 2008 peak. The most pronounced drop occurred in 2023, following the COVID-19 pandemic. This ongoing decline underscores a broader shift toward digital banking and a diminishing reliance on physical banking infrastructure throughout Europe.

# Euro Area Statistics

A wide range of aggregate euro area statistics is published on a monthly and a quarterly basis by the European Central Bank (ECB). These data can be viewed and downloaded in the statistics section of the European Central Bankswebsite Opens in new window. In addition to the euro area aggregate statistics, on the 6th December 2005 the ECB introduced new time series providing a breakdown of the national components of a range of euro area statistics. In January 2023, climate change-related indicators for the financial sector were published by the ECB for the first time as part of their climate action plan. These climate statistics, however, are published as experimental or analytical indicators owing to their limitations and should be used with care. These indicators are accessible via the links below:

*   [MFI (Monetary Financial Institutions) balance sheets: outstanding amounts Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/aggregates/bsheets/html/outstanding_amounts_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Euro area and national MFI interest rates Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/interest/interest/html/interest_rates_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Domestic and cross-border positions of MFIs (Monetary Financial Institutions): outstanding amounts Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/aggregates/cross/html/domestic_cross_border_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Official reserve assets, other foreign currency assets and related short-term liabilities Opens in new window](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/balance_of_payments_and_external/international_reserves/templates/html/201906ecb.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Euro denominated debt securities Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/securities/debt/html/debt_securities_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Euro denominated quoted shares Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/securities/quoted/html/quoted_shares_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Total assets of euro area investment funds (excluding money market funds)Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/funds/html/investment_funds_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Growth rates for the national contributions to the aggregate balance sheet of euro area monetary financial institutions Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/aggregates/bsheets/html/growth_rates_index.en.html%20 "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Climate change-related indicators Opens in new window](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/stats/cci/html/ecb.cci251127.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")

# Euro Area Statistics

A wide range of aggregate euro area statistics is published on a monthly and a quarterly basis by the European Central Bank (ECB). These data can be viewed and downloaded in the statistics section of the European Central Bankswebsite Opens in new window. In addition to the euro area aggregate statistics, on the 6th December 2005 the ECB introduced new time series providing a breakdown of the national components of a range of euro area statistics. In January 2023, climate change-related indicators for the financial sector were published by the ECB for the first time as part of their climate action plan. These climate statistics, however, are published as experimental or analytical indicators owing to their limitations and should be used with care. These indicators are accessible via the links below:

*   [MFI (Monetary Financial Institutions) balance sheets: outstanding amounts Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/aggregates/bsheets/html/outstanding_amounts_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Euro area and national MFI interest rates Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/interest/interest/html/interest_rates_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Domestic and cross-border positions of MFIs (Monetary Financial Institutions): outstanding amounts Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/aggregates/cross/html/domestic_cross_border_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Official reserve assets, other foreign currency assets and related short-term liabilities Opens in new window](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/balance_of_payments_and_external/international_reserves/templates/html/201906ecb.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Euro denominated debt securities Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/securities/debt/html/debt_securities_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Euro denominated quoted shares Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/securities/quoted/html/quoted_shares_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Total assets of euro area investment funds (excluding money market funds)Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/funds/html/investment_funds_index.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Growth rates for the national contributions to the aggregate balance sheet of euro area monetary financial institutions Opens in new window](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/money/aggregates/bsheets/html/growth_rates_index.en.html%20 "This link will open in a new tab or window")
*   [Climate change-related indicators Opens in new window](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/stats/cci/html/ecb.cci251127.en.html "This link will open in a new tab or window")

## On this page

The Eurosystem is the system of central banks of the euro area responsible for implementing the single monetary policy. It comprises the European Central Bank (ECB) and the national central banks (NCBs) of the EU member states that have adopted the euro.

From 1 January 2026 the euro area comprises twenty-one countries: **Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Spain**.

The United Kingdom was a member of the European Union from 1973 to 2020.

The **European System of Central Banks** (ESCB) is made up of the European Central Bank (ECB) and the national central banks (NCBs) of 27 EU Member States (**Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden**).

All EU countries except Denmark, which has an opt-out, are expected to join the monetary union and to introduce the euro as soon as they fulfil the convergence criteria.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TAlcFwGIQBg)

The **ECB** is an independent supranational institution with legal personality under Community law and is the centre of the ESCB and the Eurosystem. It makes sure that the tasks assigned to these institutions are performed either itself or through the NCBs, in accordance with the Statute of the ESCB/ECB. The ECB is located in Frankfurt am Main (Germany) and came into being in June 1998, replacing the European Monetary Institute (EMI).

Each NCB has legal personality under its national legislation. As an integral part of the Eurosystem, the euro-area NCBs perform the duties assigned to the Eurosystem under the rules set by the decision-making bodies of the ECB. Under their own responsibility they may perform tasks not related to the Eurosystem if the Governing Council considers they do not conflict with the objectives and tasks of the Eurosystem.

The ESCB and the ECB were set up under the terms of Article 8 of the Treaty Establishing the European Community (EC Treaty). They operate within the limits imposed by the Treaty and by the Statute of the European System of Central Banks and the European Central Bank (Statute of the ESCB/ECB), which are the primary sources of law.

## ECB's capital and reserves

The [ECB's capital](http://www.ecb.europa.eu/ecb/orga/capital/html/index.en.html) is subscribed by the NCBs of all the EU member states according to shares (**capital key**) which are calculated as the equally weighted sum of each country's share of the total GDP and total population of the European Union (see Articles 28 and 29 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB). The ECB recalculates the capital key every five years or whenever a new member joins the EU, on the basis of information provided by the European Commission. The latest adjustment took place on 1 February 2020 following the withdrawal of the United Kingdom from the EU.

The shares in the subscribed capital of the ECB are paid up in full by the Eurosystem NCBs. For the non-euro area NCBs, the ECB sets a minimum share (on 29 December 2010 this was reduced from 7% to 3.75% of the subscribed capital) as a contribution to its operational costs (see Article 47 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB).

In addition to the capital, the Eurosystem NCBs provide the ECB with a share of their foreign reserve assets, also in proportion to their capital key shares. In return, they are credited with a remunerated claim (see Article 30 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB).

The ECB can decide to increase its capital (the amount originally prescribed by Article 28 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB was EUR 5 billion) or make further calls for foreign reserve assets (the limit originally prescribed by Article 30 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB was EUR 5 billion) within the limits and according to the conditions set by the EU Council.

However, when one or more countries become EU member states and their central banks become members of the ESCB, both the subscribed capital of the ECB and the total foreign reserve assets that can be transferred to the ECB are automatically increased in accordance with Article 48 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB. Banca d'Italia's share in the subscribed capital of the ECB, as of 29 December 2020, is EUR 1,288,347,435.28, or 13.8165% of the total capital of the ECB.

The euro area NCBs paid up in full their increased subscriptions as a result of the Bank of England's withdrawal from the European System of Central Banks in two annual instalments at the end of 2021 and 2022 respectively (see [ECB press release](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2020/html/ecb.pr200130_2~59d6ffffe1.en.html "Go to the press release published on the ECB's website on 30 January 2020") published on the ECB's website on 30 January 2020).

## Monetary income

The capital key shares of the Eurosystem NCBs are also used for the allocation of the **monetary income** accruing to the NCBs as a result of their monetary policy functions (see Article 32 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB). Monetary income is defined as the net income derived from assets held against monetary liabilities (mainly banknotes in circulation and bank deposits).

Moreover, under Article 32 of the Statute the ECB settles the balances resulting from the allocation of monetary income. These balances are calculated as the difference, for each NCB, between the monetary income derived from its balance sheet and the share in the total monetary income of the Eurosystem due to it on the basis of the capital key.

## Legal acts of the ECB

Article 110 of the EC Treaty and Article 34 of the Statute of the ESCB/ECB set out the legal acts that the ECB may issue so that the ESCB can carry out its tasks.

The ECB can adopt **regulations** and **decisions**. A **regulation** has general application, is binding in its entirety, and is directly applicable in all member states. A **decision** is binding in its entirety upon those to whom it is addressed. In addition, the ECB may make **recommendations** and deliver **opinions**. These have no binding force. The Statute of the ESCB/ECB (in particular Article 14.3) also allows the ECB to adopt **guidelines** and **instructions** addressed to the national central banks of the Eurosystem. The competences and procedures for the adoption of legal acts by the ECB are set out in Article 17 of the **Rules of Procedure of the ECB**.

The [**EUR-Lex**](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/homepage.html?locale=en) website is the portal to EU legislation in general.

## On this page

*   ECB's capital and reserves
